title: Can It Survive a Bad Year?

cards.headline: Debt cuts both ways.
cards.body: Borrowed money can lift returns when business is good and sink the company when it is not. A firm can look healthy for years, then fail the season its revenue dips and a big loan comes due. Strength is about surviving the bad year.

cards.headline: Net debt, not just debt.
cards.body: Total debt alone overstates the burden — cash can pay some of it off. **Net debt** is total debt minus cash. A firm with **$2B** of debt and **$3B** of cash has **negative** net debt: it holds more cash than it owes.

cards.title: Covering the interest
cards.caption: Operating profit divided by interest owed. Sturdy covers it 8 times over; Fragile only twice, and one bad quarter could break it.

cards.prompt: Two firms carry identical debt. One holds far more cash. Equally leveraged?

options.label: Yes — the debt is the same

cards.explanation: Cash offsets debt. The cash-rich firm has lower net debt and can repay on its own terms. Judge leverage after netting out cash — and check when the debt matures.

cards.headline: Can it pay this year's bills?
cards.body: The **current ratio** is current assets over current liabilities — can near-term assets cover what's due within a year. The **quick ratio** is stricter, excluding inventory that may not sell. Below 1 warrants a look, though some efficient firms run there by design.
A single debt figure hides the risk. Four things turn it from a number into a judgment.
A company can look sound today yet stumble when a large loan reaches its [[1]] date and must be refinanced.
cards.explanation: Maturity is when the debt must be repaid or rolled over. If rates have risen or credit has tightened, refinancing can turn a healthy firm fragile overnight.

cards.headline: Safe levels are relative.
cards.body: **Net debt to EBITDA** sizes debt against operating earnings; lower is generally safer. But acceptable levels vary widely — utilities, telecoms and property firms carry far more than a software company ever should. Always compare a firm's leverage to its own industry.

cards.summary: Financial strength is surviving a bad year without forced selling.
bullets: Judge debt net of cash, and by when it's due.
Interest coverage shows if profit can service the debt.
Compare leverage within the same industry.

cards.insight: Leverage flatters returns in good years and writes the ending in bad ones. Read the balance sheet before the income statement.
